transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess… it’s this memorial I’m putting together for my brother. It started as something small, just a nice thing, you know, a few songs he liked—he had this old record he used to play, drove everyone nuts—but now it’s gotten bigger than I meant it to.

Most days I’m calling people, tracking down music, planning displays, thinking about trips and who should be there and how it ought to look. My wife says I’ve let the garden go, and I haven’t been going with my walking group, and… well, she says I’ve pushed just about everything else aside for it.
Do you feel like everything about the memorial has to be just right?

Yeah, I suppose I do, or… maybe not “perfect,” but it feels like if I leave something out, I’m letting him down. So I keep chasing little pieces—songs he liked, people who should be called, how the displays ought to look, even thinking about trips for it—and then the whole day’s gone.

My wife says I’ve pushed everything else aside. The garden’s a mess, and I haven’t been with my walking group. Funny thing, those tomatoes were actually doing pretty well this year before I got caught up in all this. But the memorial just keeps pulling me back, like there’s always one more thing I need to get right.
Do you feel like you're thinking about the memorial all the time, even when you're trying to do other things?

Yes… yes, that’s about right. I’ll be trying to do something else, and my mind just jumps—like, one minute I’m thinking about a display case, then suddenly I’m wondering if I should drive out and find this cousin nobody’s talked to in years, then I’ve got some old ballad verse stuck in my head.

And I try to write it down so I can make sense of it, but it won’t stay in order. It’s like the thoughts are moving faster than my hand. Then I remember my brother used to hum that tune when he was fixing the radio—he was always taking things apart, drove my mother crazy—and then I’m off on that, and I’ve forgotten what I was supposed to be doing.
Are you feeling overwhelmed or stressed by all the work you're putting into the memorial?

Overwhelmed… yes, I think that’s fair. It started out as just a memorial for my brother, something simple, but now most days I’m chasing down songs, calling people, figuring out displays, even thinking about trips for it.

And then I look up and the day’s gone. My wife says the garden’s been left, and I haven’t been seeing the walking group, which I used to like—there’s a fellow there who always tells the same joke about his knees—but anyway, yes, it’s gotten bigger than I meant it to, and it does feel like everything else has been pushed aside.
Do you feel like you need to control every aspect of the memorial yourself?

I don’t know if I’d say control every bit of it… but I do keep taking it back onto myself. Like, if someone else says they’ll call a person or pick a song, I start thinking, well, maybe they won’t remember the right version, or they won’t know what my brother would’ve liked.

So then I’m the one chasing down the songs, calling folks, planning the displays, even thinking about trips for it. And then the whole day’s gone. My wife says I’ve let the garden go, and I haven’t been with the walking group in a while—there’s a man there who always brings peppermint candies, funny little habit—but yes, I suppose I’ve pushed most everything else aside for this.
Has your focus on the memorial caused problems at work or in your relationships with others?

Work, no—I’m not working now, so it’s not that. But with people, yes… it has caused trouble.

I’ve missed my walking group and the book club, and the garden’s gone all wild—my wife keeps pointing that out, the tomatoes especially, though they were never as good as my father’s used to be. And at the senior center, I think I’ve upset a few people because I keep turning every conversation back to the memorial display. I don’t mean to, but someone says one thing about a song or a photo and I’m off again.

My wife says our whole day ends up being about calming me down or steering me away from another phone call, or some trip I suddenly think I need to make, or an argument over how the display should be. So… yes, it’s been hard on things between us and other people.
Are you feeling like your efforts on the memorial are taking a toll on your overall well-being?

Yes… yes, I think it is. I don’t like saying that, because the memorial feels important, you know, it’s for my brother, and he loved those old songs—there was one he used to hum when we were kids, though I can’t remember if it was from the radio or something my mother sang.

But yes, it’s taking a toll. I’ve missed the walking group, and book club too. The garden’s been let go, my wife keeps saying it’s getting away from us. And at the senior center, I think I’ve worn people out because everything I talk about turns into the memorial display somehow.

My wife says our days are all about settling me down or stopping me from making another call, or planning another trip, or getting into some argument about how it should look. So… yes, I suppose it’s affecting me more than I wanted to admit.
Do you feel guilty about something related to your brother's death that's making you put so much into the memorial?

Guilty… I don’t know. I mean, I suppose anybody thinks about what they could’ve done differently when someone dies, don’t they? But I don’t have some one thing, if that’s what you mean, like something I did or didn’t do.

It’s more… I keep thinking the memorial has to be right. Like if the songs are wrong, or the photos are in the wrong order, then people won’t remember him the way they should. He had this laugh—my brother—and there was a picture from years ago, I think at a picnic, or maybe my cousin’s place, and I keep trying to find it.

So guilt… maybe worry, maybe pressure. I’m not sure I’d call it guilt exactly.
Are you afraid that if you don't include every detail in the memorial, you will forget something important about your brother?

Afraid I’ll forget… yes, maybe that’s part of it. It’s more that the whole thing has just grown and grown. I started with wanting a nice memorial for my brother, but now I’m spending most days chasing down the right songs, calling people, thinking about photos and displays, and then I start planning some trip to find one thing or talk to someone.

And you know, my brother had opinions about music—he’d say the radio was all noise after a certain year, which my wife says I’ve started saying too much lately. But yes, I keep feeling like if I leave something out, it won’t be right somehow.

My wife says I’ve pushed everything else aside—the garden, my walking group, all of it. So I don’t know if it’s exactly fear of forgetting, but I can’t seem to stop trying to get every part of it down.
Do you think you're doing all this for the memorial because you're afraid of forgetting your brother?

Maybe… maybe that’s part of it, but I don’t know if I’d put it exactly that way. What brings me in is more that the memorial has gotten bigger than I ever meant it to. I started with just wanting something nice for my brother, and then suddenly I’m spending most days chasing down songs, calling folks, planning the display, thinking I should take a trip to find this or that.

And my wife says I’ve let everything else slide—the garden, my walking group… I used to like that walking group, there’s a fellow there who always talks about baseball, even when nobody asks him to. But I haven’t been going. It’s like everything keeps getting pulled back to the memorial.

So yes, I suppose I’m afraid of losing pieces of him, but mostly I just can’t seem to stop adding to it and working on it.
Do you feel like you can't stop thinking about the memorial even when you want to?

Yes… yes, that’s a good way of putting it. I’ll try to sit down and think, alright, just make a list, keep it sensible, and then my mind is off—first it’s the display case, then I’m wondering if I should drive out to find my cousin because he might have that one photo, then some line from an old ballad pops in, and I’m thinking maybe that should be read aloud.

It doesn’t stay in a straight line, if you know what I mean. My brother used to tease me about making lists and then losing the list—he had this little notebook he carried, always said I should get one. But now even when I write things down, it’s like I can’t get the thoughts in order fast enough. They keep jumping ahead of me.
Do you feel like you're trying to make the memorial perfect, or is it just that you can't stop thinking about it?

I don’t know that it’s perfect, exactly… I mean, maybe I want it right, but the bigger thing is I can’t stop the thoughts once they start.

My mind jumps all over. One minute I’m thinking about a display case, then I’m thinking I should take a road trip to find my cousin because he might know something, then some old ballad verse comes into my head and I think, no, that has to be in there too. And then I try to write it down, but by the time I’ve got the pen, I’m already on the next idea.

It’s like I can’t slow it down enough to put it in order.
Do you feel like you're doing all this work for the memorial because you genuinely believe it needs to be this extensive, or because you just can't seem to stop thinking about it?

I think it’s more that I can’t seem to stop thinking about it. I mean, I do want it to be good, of course, it’s for my brother—but it’s not like I sat down and said, “This has to be enormous.”

It’s more like my mind keeps jumping. One minute I’m thinking about a display case, then I’m thinking maybe I ought to take a road trip to find my cousin because he might have something important, and then suddenly there’s some old ballad verse in my head—my mother used to hum songs while she cooked, not always the same words, she’d mix them up—and then I think, well, maybe that belongs in the memorial too.

And when I try to write it in order, I can’t slow it down enough. By the time I’ve written one thing, I’m already three ideas past it.
Do you feel like you're doing these things for the memorial because you feel compelled to, or because you genuinely want to?

I suppose it’s both, but… more like I feel pulled along by it now. I did want to do something nice for my brother, genuinely. That part’s real.

But what brings me in is that it’s gotten bigger than I meant it to. Most days I’m chasing down old songs, calling people, thinking about displays, whether I should take trips to find things… and then the day’s gone. My wife says I’ve pushed aside the garden, and my walking group, and just about everything else.

I don’t know if “compelled” is the right word, but it doesn’t feel like I can just set it down and say, alright, enough for today.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop thinking about the memorial even when you try to focus on other things?

Yes… yes, that’s exactly it. I’ll try to do something else, and then my mind just jumps. Like I’ll be thinking, maybe I should just water the tomatoes or sort the mail, and then suddenly I’m back to the display case, or whether I should drive out to find my cousin because he might know something.

And then a bit of an old ballad comes in—my mother used to hum those, you know, while she was in the kitchen—and I think, wait, that verse matters somehow. So I go to write it down, but by the time I’ve got the paper, I’m already on to the next thing.

It’s not one thought, really. It’s like they’re all chasing each other, and I can’t slow them down enough to put them in order.
Do you feel like you're having thoughts about the memorial that you can't get out of your head, even when you try to think about something else?

Yes, that’s it. I try to think about something else and it won’t stay there.

It’s like my mind hops tracks—first I’m picturing a display case, then I’m thinking maybe I need to drive out and find my cousin because he might remember something, and then some old ballad verse comes up. My mother used to have all these bits of songs in her head, and she’d hum them while she was cooking, and sometimes I can almost hear the tune but not quite the words…

But yes, sorry—the memorial thoughts keep coming. I can’t slow them down enough to write them out in order. By the time I put one thing on paper, I’m already off onto the next one.
Do you feel like you're doing things for the memorial because you have intrusive thoughts that you can't ignore?

I don’t know if I’d call them “intrusive” exactly, but I can’t ignore them, no. My mind just keeps jumping.

One minute it’s the display case, then I’m thinking I ought to take a road trip to find my cousin because he might remember something, and then there’s a verse from some old ballad in my head. Those songs get tangled up with my mother humming in the kitchen, and then I’m trying to remember if it was the second verse or the third—

But yes, the point is, I can’t slow it down enough to write it in order. I try to do one thing for the memorial, and three more things come rushing in.
Do you feel like you're having thoughts about the memorial that are repetitive and unwanted?

Unwanted… I don’t know. They don’t feel like, ah, like someone else put them there. But they do keep coming back, over and over, and I can’t make them line up.

It jumps so fast—one minute I’m thinking about the display case, then I ought to go find my cousin, take a road trip maybe, because he might remember something important. Then there’s a bit of a ballad in my head, and I’m trying to catch the words before they’re gone. My mother used to hum those kinds of songs, and—

Well, yes. Repetitive, I guess. I don’t want them going so fast like that. I can’t slow it down enough to write it all in order.
Do you feel like these thoughts about the memorial are obsessive?

Obsessive… I’m not sure if that’s the right word. It’s more like my mind won’t stay on one thing.

I’ll start with the display case, and before I can finish that thought I’m thinking maybe I need to drive out and find my cousin because he’d remember some detail, and then suddenly there’s a ballad verse in my head. Then I’m trying to catch the words, and it’s already moved on again.

So, yes, they keep coming, but it feels like they’re racing more than anything. I can’t slow them down enough to write the memorial out in order.
Are these thoughts about the memorial causing you a lot of distress?

Yes… it does, though I don’t always want to admit that. It’s taken over more than I meant it to.

I’ve missed my walking group, and book club too—those were my regular things, you know, Thursdays we used to talk more about the snacks than the book half the time. And the garden’s gone wild because every time I go out there I think, “I should call so-and-so about the display,” or “maybe the senior center has room for another case,” and then I’m off on that again.

I’ve upset people there too, friends at the senior center. I keep bringing it back to the memorial, even when they’re trying to talk about something else. My wife says the whole day becomes about settling me down or stopping me from making another call, or planning some trip, or getting into an argument about how it ought to be done.

So… yes. It’s distressing. It’s like everything else is getting pushed out.
